title: Whose lane is it anyway? Why the Alberta UCP is wading into municipal issues
summary: Protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of current Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra. Yet, that same government has overruled local decision makers on a growing list of issues in the last two years…

image.caption: Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas and Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack are not happy. They say the provincial government is repeatedly stepping on the toes of cities. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Analysis

Protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of current Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra. Yet, that same government has overruled local decision makers on a growing list of issues in the last two years including bike lanes, photo radar and zoning rules.
Edmonton, Calgary mayors accuse province of overreach
Alberta’s premiers have long complained about Ottawa sticking its nose in provincial affairs.
Whether it's calling for fewer restrictions on resource development or pushing back on federal gun control, protecting provincial jurisdiction is part of Premier Danielle Smith’s mantra.

Yet, that same government has waded into a growing list of municipal issues in the last two years including bike lanes, photo radar and zoning rules. And Alberta’s big city mayors are not happy about it.
“We've seen significant overreach, overreach in a way that I've never experienced in my 13 years serving,” Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack told CBC’s West of Centre.

“I think it is time to have a real conversation about what we expect from municipalities, making sure they have the authority to address those things without this fear that you're going to have backseat drivers.”
Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, while talking with reporters last month, said the government needs to stay in its own lane.
“Overreach is bad when Justin Trudeau does it,” he said. “It’s bad when Danielle Smith does it.”
LISTEN | From bike lanes to photo radar. Alberta and its cities collide:
But tensions between cities and the province in Alberta are nothing new. The UCP jumped into local government issues multiple times since Smith won a majority mandate in 2023. Including:

items: Banning electronic tabulators in municipal elections.
Bringing in municipal political parties and allowing corporate and union donations in local elections.
Banning photo radar, a major source of revenue for municipalities.
Controlling how local taxes and development fees work, including disallowing communities like Canmore from charging a higher tax rate on some vacation properties.
Repealing all local council codes of conduct, and imposing a universal code councils must abide by.
Requiring public libraries to restrict youth access to books with sexually graphic images.
Wading into a Calgary noise bylaw, with Smith calling council the“fun police."
Legislating a provincial ability to remove municipal councillors and repeal bylaws it doesn’t like.
Stopping municipalities from using diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring decisions or mandatory training.
Preventing municipalities from accepting federal deals without provincial approval.
Requiring provincial approval on future LRT transit plans.
Granting the province the ability to remove existing city bike lanes.
Repealing Edmonton’s zoning bylaw and freezing zoning rules in Calgary.

blocks.text: Creatures of the province

The Canadian Constitution only recognizes the federal and provincial governments. The Alberta government delegates authority to cities, towns and other municipalities in the Municipal Government Act. That authority can be taken back or changed at any time.
Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams has said it’s his responsibility to set the ground rules for how municipalities operate.
But that doesn’t mean the province is following political norms.

“We absolutely are creatures of the province, but we are also a duly elected level of government,” Krista Gardner, a spokesperson for Alberta Municipalities and mayor of Calmar, a town south of Edmonton, said in an interview.

Gardner said if people are unhappy with decisions being made at local councils, they can vote differently. And if the province is dissatisfied, she’d rather see it work with councils instead of unilaterally rolling back bylaws.
At an announcement to repeal Edmonton’s zoning bylaw in October, Smith said she wants to leave municipalities to make their own decisions, but she felt compelled to act in this instance.
“When municipalities have taken actions that are undermining people’s property value, when you see the kind of reaction that we’ve seen from residents, then we have to step in,” Smith said.
But Calgary’s mayor doesn’t agree.
“It’s about power, it’s not about zoning,” Farkas told CBC last month.
Nothing to lose, columnist says
Some experts say it's not surprising the UCP is taking this approach, noting heated local issues are something the party could capitalize on.
Brendan Boyd, an associate professor of political science at MacEwan University told CBC’s Edmonton AM that it could give the party an edge among certain urban voters.

“The province is stepping in because they're going to get the support of the people who are opposed to bike lanes in the cities,” Boyd said. “And maybe that's a bit of a strategy for how they're going to set things up for the next election.”

blocks.text: Edmonton Journal columnist Keith Gerein told West of Centre that’s especially true in the capital, where the UCP has only won a single seat in the last three provincial elections.
“It's basically been an NDP fortress,” Gerein said.
“If they can walk in and be the saviour, … maybe they can swing — or they believe they can swing — a few ridings their way. It's worth a shot, right? They've got nothing to lose.”
